newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia labour market seen stalled.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia labour market seen stalled.

text.p: There is a good chance that data to be released on Thursday will show that Australia's labour market ended the 1996 year the way it began, with employment falling and unemployment rising, analysts said.
The labour market was one of the weakest areas of the economy in 1996 and this was a key factor behind the three rate cuts the Reserve Bank delivered in the second half of the year.
After two months of strong employment rises, economists expect Thursday's data will show a slight rise in employment levels, but said the risks were definitely to the downside.
The median forecast of the 30 economists Reuters surveyed was for a rise in employment of 5,000 in December. Forecasts ranged from a fall of 15,000 to a rise of 25,000.

"Whilst the economy produced nearly 50,000 jobs over October and November, this level of robustness is inconsistent with other indicators of the labour market which suggest continued softness," Societe Generale economists said in a report.
If the median forecast is realised, Australian employment will have risen by 66,600 over 1996 -- only 6,600 new jobs each month -- which equates to annual growth of just 0.8 percent.

The small jobs rise was not seen as enough to stop the unemployment rate rising. After reaching a five year low of 8.1 percent last December, unemployment moved back to 8.5 percent, a level it has since been unable to break away from.
Forecasts for December centre on an 8.6 percent unemployment rate, up slightly on November's 8.5 percent, and range from 8.3 to 8.7 percent. And the outlook does not appear too bright.

"We're starting to see some tentative growth in demand for labour, although ... that is not nearly strong enough to see the reduction in the unemployment rate that the government was hoping for," Dresdner chief economist Rob Henderson said.

The three rate cuts last year, which saw the official cash rate frop to 6.0 percent from 7.5 percent, would not show much impact on the labour market until towards the middle of the year, given that employment was a lagging indicator of activity. "We continue to see the economy fairly soft into the middle of 1997, and with employment lagging the cycle, we don't expect to see much of an improvement emerging until the middle of this year and beyond," ANZ Treasury economist Karen Pringle said.
If the labour market remains soft, calls for further interest rate cuts would intensify.

"Given the authorities' concern about unemployment, Thursday's December labour force data could have a significant impact on the likelihood, and timing, of another rate cut," Macquarie Bank economists said in a commentary.

Economists said that despite the strong recent headline jobs growth, most of the new jobs were in part time employment which created less spending power than full time jobs and therefore had less flow through effect on overall activity.
Of the almost 50,000 jobs created in October and November, 34,500 of them, or almost 70 percent, were part time.
